Ten minutes later Lord Arthur Savile burst out of Bentinck House, his face white with terror and his eyes frantic with grief. He pushed through the crowd of footmen in fur coats standing around the broad striped awning, apparently seeing and hearing nothing. The night was bitterly cold, and the gas lamps around the square blazed and flickered in the sharp wind. Yet his hands were feverishly hot, and his forehead burned like fire. He walked on and on, staggering almost like a drunken man. A policeman watched him curiously as he passed. A beggar who shuffled from an archway to ask for money recoiled at the sight of misery greater than his own. Once he stopped beneath a lamp and examined his hands. He imagined he could already see bloodstains on them, and a faint cry escaped his trembling lips.

Murder! That was what the palm reader had seen there. Murder! The night itself seemed to know, and the desolate wind seemed to howl the word into his ear. It filled the dark street corners. It grinned down at him from the rooftops.

He first reached the Park, where the somber trees seemed to draw him toward them. Exhausted, he leaned against the railings, pressing his brow to the wet metal to cool it and listening to the trembling silence among the trees. “Murder! Murder!” he repeated, as though saying it over and over could lessen the word's horror. His own voice made him shudder, yet he almost hoped that Echo would hear and rouse the sleeping city from its dreams. A wild urge seized him to stop some chance passerby and tell him everything.

Then he wandered across Oxford Street into narrow, disreputable alleys. Two women with painted faces jeered at him as he passed. Curses and blows sounded from a dark courtyard, followed by piercing screams. On a damp doorstep he saw the bent-backed figures of poverty and old age huddled together. An unfamiliar pity overtook him. Were these children of sin and misery destined for their end as he was for his? Were they too mere puppets in a monstrous spectacle?

Yet what struck him was suffering's comedy, not its mystery: its utter uselessness, its grotesque absence of meaning. How disconnected everything seemed! How completely without harmony! The gulf between the age's shallow optimism and the actual facts of existence astonished him. He was still very young.

After a while he found himself outside Marylebone Church. The silent road resembled a long ribbon of polished silver, marked here and there with the dark, intricate patterns of swaying shadows.

One day, while I was busy studying with Mr. Pocket, a note arrived in the post. Just seeing the envelope sent me into a flutter. I had never seen that handwriting before, but I guessed whose it was. There was no usual opening: no Dear Mr. Pip, Dear Pip, Dear Sir, or Dear Anything. It simply read:

“I am coming to London the day after tomorrow on the midday coach. I believe it was arranged that you would meet me? At least, Miss Havisham thinks so, and I am writing because she wishes it. She sends you her regards.

“Yours, ESTELLA.”

Given enough time, I would probably have ordered several new suits for the occasion. As there was not enough, I had to settle for the clothes I owned. My appetite disappeared at once, and I could neither rest nor find peace until the day came. Its arrival brought no relief: I was worse than ever. I began hanging around the coach office in Wood Street, Cheapside, before the coach had even left the Blue Boar in our town. Though I knew this perfectly well, I still felt it was unsafe to let the office out of my sight for more than five minutes. In this unreasonable state I had completed the first half hour of a watch that would last four or five hours when Wemmick ran into me.

“Hello, Mr. Pip,” he said. “How are you? I wouldn't have expected to find you around here.”

I explained that I was waiting for someone arriving by coach, and asked after the Castle and his aged father.

“Both doing wonderfully, thank you,” said Wemmick, “especially the Aged. He's in excellent spirits. He'll be eighty-two on his next birthday. I'm thinking of firing eighty-two shots, provided the neighbors don't complain and my cannon can stand the strain. But this isn't the sort of thing to discuss in London. Where do you think I'm going?”

“To the office?” I suggested, since he was walking that way.

“Almost,” Wemmick answered. “I'm going to Newgate prison. We're handling a case involving a banker's stolen parcel, and I've been down the road to look at where it happened. Now I need a word or two with our client.”

“Did your client carry out the robbery?” I asked.

“Good heavens, no,” Wemmick replied very dryly. “But he's accused of it. You or I might be, too. Either one of us might be accused of it, you know.”

Poor Jack was later shot by Lord Canterville in a duel on Wandsworth Common, and Lady Barbara died of a broken heart at Tunbridge Wells before the year ended. In every respect, then, it had been a great success. The costume was extremely difficult to put together, however—if I may use such a theatrical idea when discussing one of the greatest mysteries of the supernatural, or, more scientifically, the higher-natural world. His preparations took a full three hours. At last everything was ready, and his appearance pleased him greatly. The large leather riding boots belonging to the outfit were slightly too big, and he could find only one of the pair of cavalry pistols. Still, he was satisfied overall. At a quarter past one, he glided through the wooden wall panels and crept along the corridor. When he reached the twins' room, which I should mention was called the Blue Bed Chamber because of its blue hangings, he found the door slightly open. Hoping to make an impressive entrance, he threw it wide. A heavy jug of water fell straight onto him, soaking him to the skin and missing his left shoulder by only a couple of inches. At the same instant, he heard muffled shrieks of laughter from the four-poster bed. The shock was so great that he fled to his room as fast as possible. The following day he was confined to bed with a bad cold. His only comfort in the whole affair was that he had left his head behind. Had he brought it, the results might have been very serious.

He now abandoned every hope of ever frightening this ill-mannered American family. Usually he settled for creeping through the passages in soft cloth slippers, with a thick red scarf around his throat to protect him from drafts. He also carried a small old-fashioned gun in case the twins attacked. The final blow came on September 19. He had gone downstairs to the great entrance hall, confident that he could at least remain undisturbed there. To amuse himself, he was making mocking remarks about the large Saroni photographs of the United States Minister and his wife, which had replaced the Canterville family portraits. His clothing was simple but tidy: a long burial shroud dotted with graveyard soil, and a strip of yellow linen tied around his jaw to hold it shut. He carried a small lantern and a gravedigger's spade.
